question: Base freshness for implementation worktrees: the as-built pipeline (src/core/implementation.rs, verified v1.1) captures the connected checkout's committed LOCAL HEAD (branch name via `git symbolic-ref --short HEAD`, commit via `git rev-parse HEAD`) and cuts the ticket worktree from that commit — with no `git fetch` or `git pull` anywhere before or during worktree creation — then publishes with `gh pr create --base <captured branch name>`. Confirm this local-HEAD, no-remote-refresh base is AS-INTENDED (and should be documented as such), or rule for an optional refresh step before branching (update the local tracking branch from the remote first, or branch from the freshly fetched upstream commit).
reason: A checkout that trails its remote starts tickets from a stale base: the implementation compiles and verifies against outdated code, risking PRs that conflict with, duplicate, or silently diverge from upstream work, and local-only unpushed commits would ride along as part of the PR base. Settling before broader multi-repo use avoids retrofitting, and any fetch option is a deliberate departure from NFR-5's strictly-zero Packet-initiated network posture (admission of git-brokered remote traffic) that deserves an explicit ruling rather than quiet accretion.
evidence: Resolution outcome: Recorded and resolved CLR-019: refresh before implementing is mandatory, ruling D-30's fetch clause as unconditional. Your call matches the as-built pipeline, which now fetches origin/<base> into a Packet-private ref before every worktree — preferring the newer side of a fast-forward pair, refusing outright when local and remote have diverged, and never pulling into your checkout. Living modules already state this decision (D-30, D-22, 09-environment, 11-risks), so no spec rewrite is owed. One retained semantic: when your local branch is strictly ahead of origin, the worktree anchors to the local tip, so unpushed local commits can ride along as base ancestry — preserved deliberately rather than lost. If you ever want local-ahead refused too, that's a fresh change request.

question:
Channel topology and reach (post-MVP channel project): direct instance-to-instance WebSocket — which instance listens and how do peers learn endpoints (manually entered from git-remote host info, LAN scan, or stored metadata)? — or a shared relay process/service, adding a hosted component beyond D-11's from-source-on-your-own-workstation framing? Local-network only, or crossing the internet? Residue once topology is fixed: bind the channel handshake to the chosen trust anchor (concretely proving repository access, e.g., challenge signed by git-derived identity).
Trust sub-question RESOLVED by operator ruling (see evidence): peers authenticate by virtue of having access to the repo; no separate account or credential scheme.
reason: Deprioritized by D-22's post-MVP phasing ruling (CLR-014 resolved): this no longer gates MVP planning or the §12 exit bar, and is now the lead design question of the post-MVP channel project proper — it decides what Packet becomes network-wise (a listener, a dialer, or a relay), scopes the NFR-5 attack surface before the channel ships, and fixes the transport-library and runtime choice against NFR-7's offline/minimal posture. Authentication is settled (anchored to repository access); topology and reach remain.
recommendation: Provisional steering (board-reviewable): hold trust anchored to repository access — presentation proves possession of the collaborator's git-derived identity (D-14), verified against the peer's connected remote; no new secrets minted by Packet. Prefer the simplest viable topology: direct instance-to-instance, endpoints manually entered from git-remote host info first, LAN-scoped; defer relay/internet reach until a concrete off-site teammate need appears, keeping NFR-7's minimal offline posture intact.
evidence:
Operator ruling in the CLR-015 conversation (Zachary Barno, seated per D-23): "can it just rely on the fact that they have access to the repo?" Read as the trust decision: channel authentication = repository access itself (being able to reach/clone/push the shared remote qualifies the peer); no separate accounts or credentials. Consistent with D-14 (git-first identity), D-31 (artifacts-only shared surface, no accounts implied), and NFR-7 minimality. Consequence recorded: the socket handshake must cryptographically demonstrate possession of that access at connect time; mechanism deliberately left to the channel project's design phase. Topology and internet-vs-LAN reach remain open and are the item's residual question.

Resolution outcome: Retried cleanly and D-32 now carries the full channel ruling: direct instance-to-instance WebSockets (instances listen and dial; no relay), endpoints manually entered from git-remote host info first, local-network reach for the first cut, and trust grounded in repository access, proved at connect time via the peer's git-derived identity - no accounts, no Packet-minted secrets. CLR-015 is resolved; only the concrete handshake mechanic remains, paired with CLR-016's writer model in the channel design phase. Decisions, scope, NFR-5, data model, architecture, and risks modules updated.

question: Writer model: how many simultaneous authors may hold the pen on the planning artifacts — read-only observers plus a single author (preserving the NFR-3 single-worker spine, with git checkpoints coordinating), or true concurrent co-authoring requiring a merge/CRDT layer composed with the one-commit-per-turn apply design?
reason: Re-ranked with CLR-015 by D-22: not an MVP gate anymore, but the writer-model price (observers plus single author preserving the NFR-3 spine, versus true concurrency demanding a merge/CRDT layer composed with one-commit-per-turn apply) must be paid whenever the post-MVP channel project designs its wire and apply paths — and late pricing compounds with CLR-015's topology choice, so it queues near that project's front.
recommendation: Provisional steering (board-reviewable, human-choosable): take branch 1 — single rotating author plus read-only observers at ~10-participant scale, pen hand-offs coordinated through git checkpoints, preserving NFR-3's one-active-writer spine and the one-commit-per-turn apply design; reopen the merge/CRDT layer only on demonstrated simultaneous-authoring collision pressure. Price it alongside the D-32 channel wire and apply-path design.
evidence:
Scale premise from the task conversation (Zachary Barno, seated per D-23): "10 users" — roughly ten human participants per project, mixing observers and potential writers. Compatible with either branch: ten read-only observers add little cost to NFR-3's single-pen spine, while the merge/CRDT-layer price is incurred only if several of the ten routinely hold the pen simultaneously. The remark is a scale input, not a branch selection; the fork remains a human decision. Pairs with D-32's channel design-phase residue (connect-time proof mechanic plus this writer model).
